title: Dillingham Commercial Company, Inc. v. Spears
lead: A tenant’s tax and rent defaults did not forfeit its purchase option, but obtaining specific performance also required accounting for the seller’s lost use of the purchase money.

actors.name: Dillingham Commercial Company, Inc.
actors.role: Assignee of the store lease and purchase option

actors.name: Spears
actors.role: Property owner resisting exercise of the option

actors.name: Chief Justice Rabinowitz
actors.role: Author of the unanimous Alaska Supreme Court opinion

proceedings: Superior court granted summary judgment compelling sale, with purchase-price interest and insurance reimbursement, and awarded the buyer fees and costs.
Supreme Court affirmed all terms on the owner’s appeal and buyer’s cross-appeal.
limits: Sublease and insurance default arguments were waived on appeal; the buyer abandoned its insurance-reimbursement challenge.
The factual narrative gives the final tender as August 12 despite a heading’s August 17 date; no intervening event is inferred.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A store transaction includes a ten-year purchase option
sections.cue: Set out the bargain and accumulated defaults.
paragraphs: A January 15, 1967 earnest-money agreement arranged sale of Spears’s general-store business, a ten-year property lease and an option to buy the property. The March 1 lease required $600 monthly rent and payment of all taxes and assessments. During the term, if the lease was not in default, the option could be exercised by one month’s mailed notice and $20,000 toward a $79,800 price. Spears approved assignment to Dillingham Commercial Company, Inc. shortly after occupancy began.

In October 1975, Spears demanded overdue taxes within ten days and threatened foreclosure. Dillingham paid the city $16,239.61 in November, but interest, foreclosure costs and personal-property taxes remained. Spears’s March 9, 1976 letter demanded cure for delinquent taxes, insurance deficiencies and late rent. On March 22, Dillingham announced exercise of the option and offered $20,000 on May 1. Spears insisted on curing defaults first; Dillingham threatened specific performance.

After further tax demands, Spears purported on June 18 to terminate lease and option and paid the city herself. Dillingham paid additional property and personal-property taxes in July and tendered reimbursement, which Spears refused. She offered only month-to-month occupancy at $1,200. On August 12, Dillingham again tendered reimbursement, July and August rent, and the $20,000 down payment. After refusal, it sued.

sections.title: The lease survived the notice, but the option condition still mattered
sections.cue: Separate termination from equitable relief against default.
paragraphs: The superior court granted summary judgment compelling the sale. On appeal, Chief Justice Rabinowitz first explained that Spears’s notice did not itself terminate the lease. Under Klinger, Alaska’s earlier lease-termination decision, absent special agreement early termination required the prescribed judicial action and decree. Spears filed none. The lease provided Alaska-law remedies but no special unilateral-notice termination right. References to expiration “or otherwise” reasonably included judicial termination, while preserving a termination privilege despite leniency preserved only otherwise existing rights.

That did not erase the option’s no-default condition. The court separately upheld equitable relief from the tax defaults. Taxes were paid and reimbursement offered, Dillingham had paid substantial rent for nine years, and the term was nearing its end. The financial consequences made forfeiture inequitable. Installment-land-contract decisions supported discretion, though Curry showed forfeiture remained possible in extreme circumstances. An option holder had a contractual right rather than an installment purchaser’s equitable ownership, but that distinction warranted no different equitable result here.

sections.title: Long acceptance of late rent defeats forfeiture
sections.cue: Address waiver and the record assumed for summary judgment.
paragraphs: Rent had been late nearly every month, and Spears accepted it without objection until Dillingham sought to buy. The lease required written waiver and stated that delay, omission or waiver of one default did not waive another. Even such language did not invariably prevent waiver by conduct. Spears’s extended acquiescence waived reliance on late payment, and equity independently supported relief from forfeiture.

The court did not find every installment paid. Viewing the record favorably to Spears, it assumed two unpaid months. Compared with substantial rent and tax payments and prolonged absence of objection, that shortfall still did not justify forfeiture. Additional sublease and insurance grounds were undeveloped in Spears’s appellate argument and therefore waived. The trial court had also considered abandonment, seriousness and monetary cure; the appellate result did not create a blanket rule excusing those covenants.

Spears next argued that missing deed-of-trust documents left essential sale terms for trial. The superior court used the original earnest-money agreement’s payment and interest terms as part of the complete agreement insofar as consistent with the lease. She supplied no contrary evidence. The court enforced established written terms rather than inventing them. Jackson, the case she quoted for a trial requirement, concerned a disputed oral contract, a qualification absent from her quotation.

sections.title: Specific performance carries financial conditions
sections.cue: Explain why the successful buyer still owes interest.
paragraphs: The superior court required Dillingham to pay $20,016.50 purchase-price interest and $6,000 for insurance premiums including interest, while awarding it $6,710 attorney fees and $1,737.52 costs. Dillingham cross-appealed the financial conditions and fees.

The judge had mistakenly used the Rule 82 money-judgment fee schedule as though the buyer recovered the $79,800 price. Specific performance produced no money judgment, and higher assessed property value did not cure that premise. Still, $6,710 was reasonable and no clear abuse of discretion; remanding solely to reach the same proper result served no purpose. Dillingham abandoned its insurance challenge in reply and argument.

Equitable accounting placed the parties as timely performance would have done: the purchaser would have possession and income, while the seller would have the purchase money. Dillingham remained in possession. Its tender and Spears’s wrongful refusal did not let it retain both property benefits and use of the money interest-free. Interest on the full price from August 21, 1976 was proper.

Dillingham also sought credit for forty-three $600 payments deposited in trust under court order. The record did not establish their intended character, but continuing rent during possession was the most plausible explanation. The $25,800 was not a frozen purchase-money tender or full option performance and did not reduce interest.

On February 19, 1982, the Supreme Court affirmed the entire judgment. Justices Connor, Burke, Matthews and Compton joined the panel, with no separate writing. Dillingham obtained the property on the affirmed financial terms.
